title: The Assembly, the Camp, and the Neighbor's Field
summary: Moses sets rules for who may enter the assembly of the LORD, excluding some groups and welcoming Edomites and Egyptians in the third generation. He requires the war camp to be kept clean because God walks in it, forbids returning an escaped slave to his master, bans cult prostitution and interest on loans to fellow Israelites, urges care with vows, and allows a hungry traveler to eat from a neighbor's vineyard or field but not to carry the harvest away.
story: The law code of Deuteronomy continues its survey of Israel's life, moving from the household (chapters 21-22) to the boundaries of the community itself. Who belongs to the assembly that gathers before God? How must the camp be kept when God is present in it? What does neighbor love require when money is lent or a vow is made? The chapter reaches back to Israel's wilderness history, recalling Moab's hiring of Balaam in Numbers 22-24, and it reaches forward to later moments when these laws were read and argued over, from the book of Ruth, whose heroine is a Moabite, to Nehemiah's reforms after the exile.
historical:
The memory of Balaam is central to verses 3-6. According to Numbers 22-24, Balak king of Moab hired the diviner Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel on the plains of Moab, and God turned every curse into a blessing. A plaster inscription discovered in 1967 at Deir Alla in the Jordan valley, dating to about the eighth century BC, describes a seer named Balaam son of Beor who received a vision from the gods. It is not a copy of the biblical story, but it shows that Balaam was remembered in the region outside the Bible. Ammon and Moab were related to Israel through Lot (Genesis 19:36-38), and Edom through Esau, Jacob's brother, which explains why Edom is called your brother in verse 7.

The law against returning a runaway slave is remarkable in its setting. Ancient law collections generally protected owners. The Code of Hammurabi made it a capital crime to help a slave escape or to harbor one. Deuteronomy commands the opposite: the fugitive may live wherever he chooses and must not be oppressed. Most interpreters think the law refers to slaves fleeing from foreign masters into Israel's territory, though some apply it more widely.
cultural:
The assembly of the LORD (the qahal) was Israel gathered as a worshiping and governing body, not simply the population of the land. Exclusion from it did not mean expulsion from the land or from care; foreigners and resident aliens lived among Israel under the protection of its laws. The exclusion of men with damaged genitals may relate to pagan practices of ritual castration in the service of certain gods, or more generally to the requirement of wholeness in things brought near to God. The meaning of the word translated illegitimate birth in verse 2 is uncertain; Jewish tradition took it to mean the child of a forbidden union such as incest or adultery.

The shrine prostitute of verse 17 reflects a practice many scholars have linked to Canaanite fertility religion, though the extent of sacred prostitution in the ancient world is now debated, and some think the terms refer to cult functionaries more generally. The laws on interest protected poor Israelites, since loans in a farming village were usually taken out of desperation after a failed harvest, not for investment. The gleaning rule of verses 24-25 let a hungry traveler eat, while forbidding him to harvest what was not his.
literary: The chapter is a loose collection of laws linked by the theme of boundaries: who enters the assembly, what stays outside the camp, what may not come into the house of the LORD, and what may be taken from a neighbor's field. The laws of admission (verses 1-8) have a stair-step pattern, from permanent exclusion to exclusion to the tenth generation to admission in the third. The camp laws (verses 9-14) are grounded in a single theological reason: the LORD your God walks throughout your camp. The final laws are short, practical, and balanced, each giving permission and setting a limit in the same breath.

outline.t: Who may enter the assembly of the LORD
No cult prostitution or its wages
Eating from a neighbor's vineyard and field

doctrines.note: The camp must be holy because the LORD walks in it. Holiness is not only a matter of worship; it reaches into hygiene and the ordinary business of an army in the field, because God's presence is real.

The assembly of the LORD is the Old Testament's gathered people of God, and the chapter asks who belongs to it. The Greek Old Testament often translated qahal with ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church.

Neighbor love shapes economics: no interest on loans to the poor, refuge for the runaway, freedom to eat from a field when hungry but not to exploit a neighbor's work. Words spoken to God in vows are also binding.

words.note: Qahal, assembly or congregation. It means Israel gathered as God's people, whether for worship, covenant renewal, or war. The Greek Old Testament often rendered it ekklesia, which gives the New Testament its word for church and connects the church to Israel's gathered assembly.

Neshek, interest. The word comes from a root meaning to bite, a vivid picture of what interest does to a poor borrower. Israel was forbidden to charge it to a fellow Israelite, though it could be charged to a foreigner, probably a trader lending on commercial terms.

Nadar, to vow. A vow was a voluntary promise to God, often made in a time of need, to give something if God answered. Verse 22 makes clear that no one is obliged to vow, but a vow once spoken must be kept promptly.

Qedeshah, a woman associated with a shrine, usually rendered cult or shrine prostitute. The word comes from the root for holy, set apart, which is a bitter irony: what was set apart for a pagan shrine was the opposite of the holiness God required.

christ: The chapter's exclusions set up one of the Bible's great reversals. Isaiah 56:3-5 promises that the eunuch and the foreigner who hold fast to God's covenant will have a place in his house better than sons and daughters, and in Acts 8 an Ethiopian eunuch, doubly an outsider under this law, is baptized into the church. Ruth the Moabite becomes the great-grandmother of David and appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). In Christ, Paul writes, those who were far off have been brought near (Ephesians 2:13). Jesus' disciples plucked heads of grain as they walked through fields (Mark 2:23), which verse 25 allowed; the dispute with the Pharisees was about the Sabbath, not theft. Jesus also taught that his followers should need no oaths, but let their yes be yes (Matthew 5:33-37), carrying the concern of verses 21-23 for truthful speech.

hard.q: If Moabites were excluded from the assembly, how could Ruth the Moabite become an ancestor of David?
hard.a:
The book of Ruth tells of a Moabite woman who married into Israel and became David's great-grandmother, which seems to clash with verse 3. Several answers have been given. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Mishnah, read the law as excluding Moabite men but not Moabite women, noting that the reason given (not meeting Israel with food and water) described what men would have done. Others note that the law concerns entering the assembly, the gathered worshiping and governing body, not marriage or residence in Israel. Still others read Ruth as a deliberate counterpoint, a story showing that faithful love and loyalty to Israel's God can open doors the law had closed.

The tension was real in Israel's own history. After the exile, Nehemiah read this passage aloud and separated from Israel those of foreign descent (Nehemiah 13:1-3), while the book of Ruth kept alive the memory of a Moabite who belonged. The Bible holds both, and the prophets and the New Testament move toward a people of God gathered from every nation.

questions: The camp had to be holy because God walked in it. What would change in your daily life if you took God's presence there seriously?
Israel was forbidden to return a runaway slave. Who are the people fleeing hardship today, and what would it mean not to oppress them?
The law allowed a hungry person to eat from a field but not to fill a basket. Where is the line in your life between meeting need and taking advantage?
